title: Domain-Specific Inhibitory Control Training to Improve Children’s Learning of Counterintuitive Concepts in Mathematics and Science
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether children’s inhibitory control (IC) is related to learning counterintuitive concepts in mathematics and science, and whether IC can be improved through a domain-specific classroom intervention. The authors argue that misconceptions and misleading perceptual cues interfere with children’s understanding of science and mathematics, and that training children to “stop and think” may help them inhibit intuitive but incorrect responses.

The study had two parts. First, the authors conducted cross-sectional analyses with 627 primary school children in Years 3 and 5 in London schools, examining associations among IC, counterintuitive reasoning, and standardized mathematics and science achievement. Second, they evaluated a computer-based intervention called Stop & Think, delivered either as a teacher-led whole-class activity or a pupil-led individual activity during mathematics and science lessons over 10 weeks. The software embedded IC prompts, scaffolded practice, and virtual peer explanations within curriculum-based math and science content.

Results showed that children frequently selected misconception-based answers on the counterintuitive reasoning task, and that better IC was associated with better counterintuitive reasoning and higher academic achievement. The intervention produced evidence of near transfer for Year 3 children on counterintuitive reasoning in both delivery modes, and teacher-led Stop & Think also improved Year 3 science achievement. Effects were weaker or absent for Year 5 and no transfer was found to the Stroop-like IC measure. The authors conclude that domain-specific IC training embedded in curriculum content may support science and mathematics learning, but the evidence is preliminary and effects vary by age and delivery mode.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental classroom study with baseline/post measures, but conditions were not fully randomized and some outcome data were missing by condition. It is stronger than purely correlational work, yet has notable internal-validity limitations.
impact_tier_rationale: The intervention shows small-to-moderate gains on near-transfer counterintuitive reasoning in Year 3 and a modest science-achievement effect (ηp²=.077), but results are inconsistent across age groups and delivery modes. Overall impact appears promising but limited and context-specific.

interventions.use_case: Classroom-based computerised practice called Stop & Think that embeds inhibitory-control prompts within mathematics and science curriculum content, delivered either teacher-led on an interactive whiteboard or pupil-led on individual computers.

finding.finding_summary: Children showed strong baseline misconceptions in mathematics, with Year 3 making significantly more misconception than other errors (t(350)=20.76, p<.001, d=1.11) and Year 5 also showing this pattern (t(242)=2.38, p=.018, d=0.15). The intervention improved mathematics achievement only weakly/inconsistently: Year 3 showed no significant effect for mathematics achievement, while Year 5 pupil-led Stop & Think showed a small effect that did not survive Bonferroni correction (F(1,124)=4.85, p=.029, ηp²=.038).
finding.measure: Counterintuitive reasoning test (mathematics items); Progress Test in Mathematics 7/9
finding.study_size: n=594 baseline reasoning; n=283 achievement; intervention subsamples varied

finding.finding_summary: Children also showed strong baseline misconceptions in science, with Year 3 making more misconception than other errors (t(350)=12.89, p<.001, d=0.69) and Year 5 showing the same pattern (t(242)=11.02, p<.001, d=0.71). Stop & Think produced a significant gain in Year 3 teacher-led science achievement relative to teaching as usual (F(1,64)=5.37, p<.05, ηp²=.077), but there was no significant science-achievement effect for Year 5 pupil-led delivery.
finding.measure: Counterintuitive reasoning test (science items); Progress Test in Science 8/9
finding.study_size: n=594 baseline reasoning; n=129 achievement; intervention subsamples varied

finding.finding_summary: The intervention targeted inhibitory control as a domain-specific support for counterintuitive reasoning, but it did not improve the separate Stroop-like inhibitory-control measure overall. At baseline, inhibitory control was associated with better counterintuitive reasoning and achievement, and the intervention improved near-transfer counterintuitive reasoning in Year 3 (STT ηp²=.067; STP ηp²=.041), suggesting gains in applied reasoning/self-regulation rather than the generic IC task.
finding.measure: Stroop-like inhibitory-control task; counterintuitive reasoning test
finding.study_size: n=451 baseline IC; intervention subsamples varied
finding.effect_size: baseline r up to .33; intervention ηp²=.067/.041; no overall IC effect
